# Turkey Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/turkey-facts-for-kids/

These odd-looking birds with colorful fleshy heads and wattles grace tables nationwide celebrating Thanksgiving. But wild turkeys thrive throughout impressive ranges and adapt to varied habitats beyond just gracing holiday meals. Explore turkey traits kids relate to, from their wingspan sizes, speed running on strong legs, and bizarre mating displays. Learn amazing trivia how these peculiar poultry birds fit into backyards and wilderness areas alike.

- Male turkeys called toms sport vivid red, white and blue facial wattles while females show smaller paler warty head parts named hens lack.

- Their odd fleshy bumps called caruncles rattling alarm most birds signal these ground birds instead collect mating displays.

- Turkey bare heads simply featherless bright skin projecting nodules aiding temperature regulation through sizable blood volumes cooled circulated during summer heat waves.

- No significant differences size between males females turkeys contradicting natural world trends although males appear substantially larger puffing feathers chasing mating rituals.

- They boast expansive five foot (1.5 m) wingspans balancing nearly 20 pound (9 kg) heft for hardy powerful soaring flight reaching 50 mph (80 kph).

- Constant murmuring, chattering turkey congregations socialize together while specific yelps, cuts, purrs, cries, cackles and gobbles hold meaning.

- Their poor vision estimating distances offsets heightened summer scent glands seeking mates plus excellent low-light night capabilities evolved when majority predators hunt.

- Groups adults young turkey offspring called broods forage together remaining partially into following year learning survival skills mimicry steadily.

- Open forests near fields allowing grazing insects and seeds collected sustain turkeys well when coupled abundant ground scratching opportunities.

- Native Americans hunted wild turkeys first with colonists noticing flocks dots skies flocking between trees initially. Forest clearances allowing farmland spiked growth.

- Conscious conservation attempts rebounded turkeys from extinction early 1900s after excessive hunting habitat losses jeopardized sustainability severely until coordinated restoration policies reversed declines regionally.

- Today’s worldwide 9 million wild turkey populations thrive recovering spreading territories broadly. 4.2 million overpopulated Alaska alone. Reintroduction programs successful.

- Introducing competitive exotic pheasants for hunting purposes complicated management forcing mild ingenious compromises safeguarding distinct species conflicting. Turkeys admirably held their own reasonably well comparatively.

- Every courtship begins male turkeys puffing feathers strutting while tipping beaks skyward emitting screams grabbing attention potential mates responds.

- Their gobble vibrato call projects mile distracting any challenging competition amongst tree stands conveying fitness desirability suitability towards visiting females urged approaching displays.

- Surviving chicks follow mothers closely copying feeding techniques eight weeks who defend them aggressively hissing expanded wings fearsome sights against deadly egg seeking predators.

- dogged persistence bonds brooding turkey pairs together annually despite only one in twenty eggs reaching sustainable winter flock integration highlighting relentless reproductive devotion ingrained.

- Turkey wing bones contain struts supporting substantial heft generating lift required fleeing predators given their preference roosting high tree branches rather ground dwelling.

- Keen visions noticing slightest forest movements serve them well when evading hunters. Realize you first likely. Reputations extreme wary cleverness persists for good reason!

- They sprint fleet-footed 25 mph (40kph) dodging threats rather confronting attackers forcefully. Their survival always remains fleeing confronting unnecessary danger pointlessly.

- When cornered turkeys bluff band together bullying intense hostile aggression facing assailants. Unprepared hikers surprised groups in forests unexpectedly can become hazardous themselves behaving threateningly.

- Opportunistic Turkey diets incorporate berries, nuts, fruits, seeds, insects or worms although grassy vegetation constitutes 80% intake allowing thriving varied landscapes abundantly.

- Scratching brush piles uncovering hidden caches acorns when discovering becomes impossible simply relocates towards greener pastures provided resolving feeding hurdles, utilizing ingenuity and intellect impressively.

- Captive turkeys, overfed grain rations preparing holiday feasts, contrasts naturally leaner muscular counterparts living actively surviving harsher wild conditions very differently.

- Their spring scavenging baby snake eggs seems savage, although utilizes abundant protein benefiting next generations chicks tremendously. Sustaining future bloodlines overrides squeamishness reasonably.

- Turkeys cared properly interact affectionately with handlers enjoying physical touch, establishing emotional bonds beyond simply satisfying food requirements expectantly.

- Legendary turkey intelligence manifest itself escaping perceived dangers way recognizing hunters camouflage, realizing dangers awaiting investigating specific calls and responding accordingly repeatedly.

- Some turkeys stamped feet signaling offspring follow them towards safer grounds or away external hazards concern. Researchers studied communication vocal tones verifying fowl basic language advancements scientifically recently.

- Turkey groups sleep together in branches or on the ground for warmth and predator protection after analyzing safer roosting location options thoughtfully.

- By pretending injured wings seeking quick shelter shrubs, mother turkeys cleverly lure stealth predators from discovering hidden vulnerable offspring huddling nearby instinctively reactively. Their parental devotion extends tremendous risks personally ensuring next generations thrive realistically.

## FAQ

How fast can wild turkeys run? Surprisingly quick, wild turkeys sprint steadily around 25 mph (40 kph) and may reach short bursts of 55 mph dodging threats when pressed into evasion.

Do turkeys care for their young? Yes, mother turkeys are very protective and nurturing teaching essential skills during the first 2 months until juvenile independence. They make shrill alarm calls and defend their brood aggressively if threatened.

Why do turkeys have wattles? The odd flesh features called wattles and other protruding parts called caruncles likely developed helping regulate excess body heat, circulating blood volumes for cooling effects. Their uses remain uncertain beyond mutations remaining tolerable characteristics.

Which conservation laws help wild turkeys? Early 20th century hunting and habitat loss almost eradicated them. Sensible foresting laws, hunting limits and wildlife area protections allow populations today thriving around 7 million in North America. Reintroduction programs proved hugely successful.

Do wild turkeys flock together? Yes, turkeys form extended social flocks usually local family groupings foraging together. Juveniles stay within a brood learning survival skills nearly 2 years before dispersing when mature mixing adult flocks eventually.

# Moon Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/moon-facts-for-kids/

Gazing up at the glowing night sky, Earth’s lone orbiting satellite captivates kids and adults alike with its allure, mystery, and natural wonder. The moon holds so many intriguing secrets spanning its craters, phases, landings, mythology and more just waiting to be uncovered. Learn all about what makes the moon such an enthralling astronomical highlight among planets with these cool facts for children.

## Moon Facts for Kids

- The moon is approximately 238,855 miles (384,400 km) from Earth on average, circling us every 27.3 days.

- Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei observed the moon’s craters and valleys in 1609 using an early telescope, describing features dramatically differing ideas at the time.

- Twelve American astronauts comprising of eleven men and one woman have walked on the moon cumulatively to date during NASA’s Apollo space program between 1969 through 1972.

- The same side of the moon always faces Earth since the natural satellite rotates precisely once per orbit. This phenomenon is known as being tidally locked.

- Lunar eclipses create a “blood moon” red coloring from sunlight refracting onto the moon’s surface by passing first through Earth’s atmosphere.

- Since the moon lies closer to Earth than the International Space Station, unprotected astronauts must wear specialized spacesuits while walking on the moon’s surface potentially experiencing temperature extremes over 200°F.

- Mythology and ancient stories from Greek, Roman and Norse civilizations feature moon gods and goddesses representing lunar power believed driving humans occasionally mad. This temporary inflicted madness became known as lunacy.

- The moon likely formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago according to scientific theories, just 60 million years following Earth’s creation.

- Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin narrated the first moonwalk in July 1969 which Armstrong claimed was “…one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind” televised for 600 million viewers.

- Without the moon stabilizing tilt, Earth could wobble unpredictably on its axis, severely fluctuating climate temperatures and conditions over seasons.

- Since lower gravity generates less friction and air resistance, objects fall slower on the moon compared to Earth. Feathers and bowling balls dropped together land simultaneously.

- The moon’s craters, valleys and mountains stem from extreme heating underway billions of years ago from asteroid bombardment and volcanic eruptions rather than wind and water erosion forces shattering land here.

- Sophisticated lunar laser ranging experiments bounce light beams between observatories worldwide and reflectors left on the moon precisely charting minute fluctuations in astronomical distances between Earth and moon.

- Ancient tribes and civilizations monitored lunar phases closely for timing spiritual rituals while farmers find new and full moons useful predicting sowing and reaping crops respectfully.

- Over long periods, the moon’s gravitational pulls produce land tide bulges spanning 20 inches temporarily shifting dirt while additional ocean tide flows exceed 30 feet.

- Impacts creating craters and asteroids pummeling the moon’s surface causes bright hot glowing molten splashes radiating out from chaotic contact points clearly observable using telescopes.

- The Apollo astronauts’ footprints and rover tire tracks sit undisturbed on the airless, erosionless moon where footfalls imprinted that July 20th, 1969 day eternally.

- Unity, Tranquility, Serenity and Harmony represent appropriately descriptive names for select Apollo lunar landing sites conveying otherworldly states of grace astronauts encountered there.

- Moon rocks contain surprising traces of hydrogen theorized originating from solar winds bonding to common oxygen somehow not explains fully.

- Over 4-billion-year bombardments, innumerable meteoroids striking moons mountains and craters bears unmistakable testimony of intense early fierce asteroid pelting lacking protective atmosphere.

- 17th century thinker Copernicus studied lunar craters and peaks concluding similar land formations means Earth and moon share common cosmic origins alike.

- Looming lunar eclipses where sunlight rays indirectly paint moons fully shadowed face haunting blood red occurs moments moon passes directly behind Earth.

- Neil Armstrong carried assorted international commemorative medallions cautiously onto moon intending installation completing ultimate symbolic gesture celebrating monumental achievement occasion.

- Echoing Neil Armstrong’s words, a plaque attached Eagle lander reads, “We came in peace for all mankind.” underscoring humanity’s unified wonder and goodwill exemplified gloriously.

- Deceptively, nearby full moons appear vastly larger near horizons merely because optical depth perception falters without usual framed references allowing our eyes misinterpreting scale.

- Mickey Mouse accompanies 13 ounces Moon rocks 220 experts nationwide receiving hoax version materials meticulously created by NASA encouraging chemical analysis skills improving knowledge founded through scientific process over wishful thinking.

- Speculation suggests potentially ice harvesting from lunar poles digging 6 feet deep could provide self-sufficient water resources essential for establishing permanently inhabited moon exploration bases studiously.

- Solemnly carrying recognized moon walker Neil Armstrong’s ashes secretly, his Apollo 11 crew member Buzz Aldrin romantically rejoined colleague above during 2012 memorial departure service years afterwards symbolically.

- Imbued intensive focus and lighthearted moments amid divisions dark vastness isolation three Apollo 17 representatives spent longest periods exploring moon December 1972 later inspiring future generations return undaunted.

- The 50-year Apollo program conducted achieving President Kennedy’s 1961 bold vision exploring moon remains remarkable displaying humanity’s unwavering godly quest satiating boundless imaginations when organized virtuously coordinated through faith, wisdom and willpower ultimately.

## Moon Facts for Kids FAQ

How old is the moon? Scientific theories deduce the moon likely formed 4.53 to 4.51 billion years ago early in Earth’s development about 60 to 130 million years after solar system creation.

What causes moon phases seen from Earth? The lunar phase cycle arises from variable illuminated portions that sunlight strikes as the moon orbits Earth over 27.3 days from fresh through waxing, full, waning and repeating stages.

Why does the same moon face always point toward the Earth?
The moon experiences gravitational tidal locking with Earth so identical lunar hemispheres perpetually orient planetward as it pirouettes mid orbit over 29.5 day full rotational periods creating the phenomenon.

Who was the first woman to walk on the moon? American Apollo Astronaut Sally Ride trained intensely for moonwalking but unfortunately no female stepped moon soil yet through 2022 although NASA plans targeting future manned lunar exploration inclusive commitments currently.

How many moon landings were there? In total six successful crewed NASA Apollo landings occurred between 1969 through 1972 ferrying 12 astronauts safely walking upon lunar surfaces through Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17 missions each contributing valuable rock samples and photography documenting achievements extensively.

# 30 Giraffe Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/giraffe-facts-for-kids/

Standing tall as the tallest mammals on land, giraffes capture our imagination with their extraordinary height, elegant walking style, and unique spotted coats. These majestic animals have several surprising traits that fascinate young explorers. Discover amazing tidbits about these peaceful, leaf-eating giants of the African savanna that kids will love learning in this list of giraffe facts for children.

## Giraffe Facts for Kids

- Male giraffes use their long necks like a weapon, swinging them to strike opponents with their hard ossicones (horn-like growths on their heads).

- A giraffe’s habitat range in Africa includes savannas, grasslands or open woodlands. Their favorite leaves grow on tall acacia trees.

- Giraffes only need 5 to 30 minutes of sleep in a 24 hour period! They often achieve that in quick power naps.

- Newborn calves are 6 feet tall and can stand just within the first hour after birth.

- Since a giraffe’s heart must pump blood upward roughly 8 feet to reach their brain, it evolved to weigh 24 pounds (11 kg) and their blood pressure is twice what a human’s is.

- Giraffes run up to 35 miles per hour (56 kph) in quick bursts and steadily cruise at 10 mph (16 kph).

- Giraffes have bluish-purple tongues which are tough and covered in bristly hair to help them feed on thorny plants without injury.

- Male giraffes use their tongues to pull tasty leaves off branches into their mouths. Females simply eat around the thorns.

- A giraffe’s front and back legs bear weight equally despite the difference in leg length. Their lower front legs adapt by having thicker, more vertical bones.

- Giraffes have never been captured yawning in the wild or captivity. No one knows why they don’t!

- Despite their vocal anatomical structures, giraffes do not produce any true calls, grunts or roars. Just flute-like whistles you must stand fairly close to hear.

- A giraffe calf can stand up within 30 to 60 minutes after birth. These gangly youngsters are 6 feet tall at birth from hoof to shoulder.

- Giraffes have only four basic gaits: walk, trot, canter and gallop. They spend nearly half their time feeding moving at a walk, with occasional faster bursts.

- A giraffe eats hundreds of pounds of leaves each week. Their 18-inch (46 cm) prehensile tongue helps them forage.

- Mature bulls develop calcium growths called ossicones atop their heads which they use during “neck fights” establishing hierarchy for mating rights.

- Traditionally the existence of giraffe vocalizations was questioned, but they actually hum, whistle, snort and hiss in addition to calf bleating noises.

- The modern giraffe species evolved from a shorter, deer-like ancestor called the sivatherium which became extinct over a million years ago.

- Giraffes feature a spotted pattern with jagged edges unique to each individual like a human fingerprint to identify young. No two giraffes have exactly matching coats.

- Their 6 inch (15 cm) tongues are tough enough to trim back acacia trees’ vicious thorns then deftly select choice leaves seemingly without harm while feeding.

- Giraffes always have their lower lip curled under when feeding to discreetly lick leaves straight into their mouths, then regurgitate cud later for final chewing.

- A giraffe heart measures 2 feet (60 cm) long and weighs 24 lbs (11 kg), generating tremendous force to pump blood up their extremely long necks to the brain.

- Giraffes can completely close their muscular nostrils to seal out blowing dust as well as parasites at times.

- Their hooves measure 12 inches (30 cm) across for stability on long legs holding nearly 2 tons split over their front and back feet equally.

- Giraffes sport a short furry mane along neck tops, an evolutionary relic from heavily maned ancestors called sivatherium now extinct over one million years.

- These giants evolved smaller brains over time since blood pumping requirements to oxygenate tissues outweighs added cranial demands for complex neural wiring benefiting intelligence.

- Yellow-ish patches contrasting their darker fur act as primitive camouflage visually breaking the body outline amid Africa’s tan bushveld terrain stealthily despite massive heights approaching 19 feet.

- Giraffe fur feels coarse with unusual 8-sided ossicones (bony protrusions) atop male heads used sparring over mating rights with females, establishing hierarchy through “necking” battles.

- Their prehensile 18 inch (46 cm) tongue grasp even thorny acacia tree shoots deftly, drawing choice leaves into protected mouths. This flexible adaptation allows exploiting vegetation other grazers cannot access.

- Giraffes sport the longest tail hairs in the animal kingdom, measuring over 8 feet (2.4 m) long used as flyswatters batting insects away from uteruses while birthing new calves cautiously.

- Despite tremendous dimensions with relatively few predators, giraffes average lifespans under 25 years from natural environmental challenges making their existence seem fleeting.

## FAQ About Fun Giraffe Facts

What is a baby giraffe called? A baby giraffe is called a calf. Newborns are about six feet tall at birth!

Why do giraffes have long blue tongues? Giraffes evolved long bluish-purple tongues covered in thick bristly hair allowing them to feed on nutritious yet thorny acacia tree leaves other animals cannot reach comfortably.

How fast can a giraffe run? Giraffes can sustainably run 10 miles per hour (16 kph) but reach breathtaking bursts nearing 35 mph (56 kph) pace if needed to outrun predators for short distances despite towering heights.

Why are giraffes tongues dark purple? Uncertain scientifically, but giraffes bluish-back tongues supply blood richly supporting dedicated opportunistic feeding on thorny vegetation most mammals cannot consume, suggesting the unusual hue indicates an exceptionally prehensile, durable and thickly haired adaptation.

What country has the most giraffes? Kenya features America’s densest last remaining wild herds roaming protected savannah preserves cautiously avoided poachers seeking illegally trafficked tail hairs, hides and scales sustaining esteemed traditional folk remedies globally. Over 100,000 remain continentally.

# What Does Skidamarink Mean?
URL: https://plooshi.com/what-does-skidamarink-mean/

The charming and whimsical word “Skidamarink” has delighted generations of children and parents alike. This term, originating from a children’s song of the same name, is a beautiful example of how language can evoke feelings of warmth and affection, even without a concrete meaning. While “Skidamarink” doesn’t have an official definition in the English language, its use in the song context has always been associated with expressions of love and affection, akin to saying “I love you” in a playful and tender way.

History of “Skidamarink”

Tracing back to the early 20th century, “Skidamarink” first made its appearance in the 1910 Broadway musical, “The Echo.” However, it wasn’t until later that it was adapted into the children’s song that is now known and loved around the world. The song’s catchy melody and simple, heartfelt lyrics have made it a staple in preschools and children’s TV shows.

Understanding the Lyrics

The lyrics of “Skidamarink” are simple yet captivating. They typically go, “Skidamarink a dink a dink, Skidamarink a doo, I love you.” This repetition and playful sound make it an instant hit among children, effectively conveying feelings of love and happiness. The nonsensical nature of the word adds to its charm, making it fun and easy for children to sing and express affection.

Conclusion

“Skidamarink” is a nonsensical, endearing term made popular by the children’s song “Skidamarink.” It doesn’t have a specific meaning but is generally understood to convey affection and love, similar to terms like “I love you” in the song’s context.

# Elephant Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/elephant-facts-for-kids/

Elephants are the biggest animals that live on land, and they are also some of the smartest! With their long trunks, floppy ears and gentle ways, elephants live in close families and take great care of their babies. Let's stomp into some amazing elephant facts!

- Animal type: Mammal
- Home: Grasslands and forests of Africa and Asia
- Food: Grass, leaves, bark, fruit and roots (they are herbivores)
- Size: Up to about 13 feet (4 m) tall at the shoulder
- Life span: About 60 to 70 years in the wild

## Facts
- There are three kinds of elephants: the African savanna elephant, the African forest elephant and the Asian elephant.
- African savanna elephants are the largest land animals on Earth.
- An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip joined together.
- A trunk has tens of thousands of muscles, so it can pick up something as tiny as a peanut.
- Elephants use their trunks to smell, breathe, drink, grab food, hug and say hello.
- An elephant can suck up several liters of water into its trunk and then squirt it into its mouth.
- Elephants love to spray water and dust on their backs to stay cool and protect their skin from the sun.
- Tusks are really very long teeth that keep growing for the elephant's whole life.
- African elephants have big ears shaped a bit like the continent of Africa, while Asian elephants have smaller, rounder ears.
- Flapping their huge ears helps elephants cool down on hot days.
- Elephants eat for up to 16 to 18 hours a day.
- An adult elephant can eat around 150 kilograms (over 300 pounds) of food in a single day.
- Elephants live in family groups called herds, led by the oldest and wisest female, called the matriarch.
- A baby elephant is called a calf.
- A newborn elephant calf can weigh around 100 kilograms (more than 200 pounds)!
- Mother elephants are pregnant for almost two years, longer than any other mammal.
- Baby elephants sometimes suck their trunks, a little like human babies suck their thumbs.
- Elephants talk to each other with trumpets, rumbles and very low sounds that people can't even hear.
- Elephants can feel rumbling sounds through the ground with their sensitive feet.
- Elephants have amazing memories and can remember friends and places for many years.
- Elephants can recognize themselves in a mirror, which only a few animals can do.
- Elephants walk on their tiptoes, with a thick cushion of fat in each foot to soften every step.
- Elephants can't really jump, but they are good swimmers and can use their trunks like snorkels.
- An elephant's skin can be about 2.5 centimeters (1 inch) thick in places, but it is still sensitive to bug bites and sunburn.
- Elephants are endangered, so people around the world work hard to protect them and their homes.

## Questions
Q: How big is an elephant?
A: African savanna elephants can stand about 10 to 13 feet (3 to 4 m) tall at the shoulder and weigh as much as a big truck, around 6,000 kilograms (13,000 pounds) for a large male.
Q: What do elephants eat?
A: Elephants are herbivores. They eat grass, leaves, twigs, bark, roots and fruit, and they spend most of the day eating.
Q: Why do elephants have trunks?
A: A trunk is a long nose and upper lip that works like a hand. Elephants use it to breathe, smell, drink, eat, lift things and greet their family.
Q: Do elephants really never forget?
A: Elephants have excellent memories. They remember water holes, paths and other elephants for many years, which helps the herd survive.
