# Penguin Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/penguin-facts-for-kids/

Penguins are birds that can't fly, but they are superstar swimmers! In their tuxedo-like feathers, penguins waddle on land and zoom through the water to catch fish. Let's slide into some cool penguin facts!

- Animal type: Bird
- Home: Coasts and oceans of the Southern Hemisphere, from Antarctica to near the equator
- Food: Fish, krill and squid
- Size: From about 16 inches (40 cm) to 4 feet (1.2 m) tall
- Life span: About 15 to 20 years

## Facts
- There are about 18 kinds of penguins.
- Almost all penguins live in the southern half of the world, not at the North Pole.
- The emperor penguin is the biggest penguin and can stand about 4 feet (1.2 m) tall.
- The little penguin (also called the fairy penguin) is the smallest, at only about 16 inches (40 cm) tall.
- Penguins can't fly, but their wings work like flippers to help them swim.
- Some penguins can swim about 22 miles per hour (35 km/h) in short bursts.
- Emperor penguins can dive deeper than 500 meters (over 1,600 feet) looking for food.
- A penguin's black-and-white feathers are camouflage: the dark back blends in with deep water from above, and the white belly blends in with the bright surface from below.
- Penguins have lots of tightly packed feathers plus a layer of fat to stay warm.
- Penguins sometimes slide on their bellies across the ice. This is called tobogganing!
- Penguins drink salt water, and special glands above their eyes help get rid of the extra salt.
- Penguins eat fish, squid and tiny shrimp-like animals called krill.
- A group of penguins on land is called a colony or a rookery.
- Some penguin colonies have hundreds of thousands of birds.
- Every penguin has its own voice, so parents and chicks can find each other in a noisy crowd.
- Emperor penguin dads balance the egg on their feet and keep it warm under a flap of skin for about two months.
- During that time, emperor penguin dads don't eat at all.
- Emperor penguins huddle together in big groups to share warmth during freezing Antarctic storms.
- Baby penguins are called chicks, and they are covered in fluffy down feathers.
- Gentoo penguins are known as the fastest-swimming penguins.
- Some male penguins give a female a special pebble to help build their nest.
- Galapagos penguins live near the equator, where it is warm.
- Penguins molt once a year, losing all their old feathers and growing new ones.
- Penguins can't breathe underwater, so they pop up to the surface for air.
- Climate change and overfishing are making life harder for some penguins, so many people work to protect them.

## Questions
Q: Can penguins fly?
A: No. Penguins are birds, but their wings have turned into strong flippers that help them 'fly' through the water instead of the air.
Q: Where do penguins live?
A: Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere: Antarctica, South America, Africa, Australia, New Zealand and even the Galapagos Islands near the equator.
Q: What do penguins eat?
A: Penguins eat fish, squid and krill. They catch their food by diving and swimming fast underwater.
Q: Why are penguins black and white?
A: Their colors are camouflage. From above, their dark backs blend in with the deep ocean, and from below, their white bellies blend in with the bright water surface.

---

# Octopus Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/octopus-facts-for-kids/

Octopuses are clever ocean animals with eight wiggly arms and no bones at all! They can change color in the blink of an eye, squeeze through tiny holes and even solve puzzles. Let's dive into some amazing octopus facts!

- Animal type: Mollusk (cephalopod)
- Home: Oceans all around the world
- Food: Crabs, shrimp, clams and fish
- Size: From less than 1 inch to over 16 feet (5 m) across, depending on the kind
- Life span: About 1 to 5 years

## Facts
- An octopus has eight arms covered in suction cups.
- There are around 300 kinds of octopuses.
- Octopuses have no bones, so they can squeeze through any hole bigger than their beak.
- An octopus has a hard beak, a little like a parrot's, that it uses to eat.
- Octopuses have three hearts!
- An octopus has blue blood.
- Octopuses can change the color and even the bumpy texture of their skin to hide.
- When an octopus is scared, it can squirt a cloud of dark ink and zoom away.
- Octopuses swim by shooting water out of a tube called a siphon, like a little jet.
- Each suction cup can taste and feel what it touches.
- Much of an octopus's brainpower is in its arms, so each arm can explore on its own.
- If an octopus loses an arm, it can grow a new one.
- Octopuses are very smart and can open jars, solve mazes and use tools.
- Some octopuses carry coconut shells to use as a hiding place.
- The giant Pacific octopus is the biggest kind and can be over 16 feet (5 m) across.
- Some octopuses are smaller than your fingernail.
- The blue-ringed octopus is small but very venomous, so people should never touch it.
- The mimic octopus can copy the shapes of other sea animals, like lionfish and sea snakes.
- Octopuses love crabs, shrimp, clams and fish.
- Octopuses usually live alone in dens made of rocks or shells.
- A mother octopus guards her eggs and keeps them clean until they hatch.
- Baby octopuses are called hatchlings, and many are as small as a grain of rice.
- The plural of octopus can be 'octopuses' or 'octopodes' (but not really 'octopi').
- Octopuses have lived in the oceans since long before the dinosaurs.
- Octopuses mostly hunt at night and rest during the day.

## Questions
Q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
A: An octopus has three hearts. Two pump blood through the gills, and one pumps blood to the rest of the body.
Q: Do octopuses have bones?
A: No. Octopuses have soft bodies with no bones. The only hard part is their beak, which is why they can squeeze through tiny spaces.
Q: Why do octopuses squirt ink?
A: Ink makes a dark cloud that confuses predators, giving the octopus time to escape.
Q: Are octopuses smart?
A: Yes! Octopuses are among the smartest animals without a backbone. They can solve puzzles, open jars and remember tricks.

---

# Butterfly Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/butterfly-facts-for-kids/

Butterflies are beautiful insects with colorful wings that flutter from flower to flower. They start life as tiny eggs, then become hungry caterpillars before turning into butterflies. Let's flutter into some fun butterfly facts!

- Animal type: Insect
- Home: Every continent except Antarctica
- Food: Flower nectar (caterpillars eat leaves)
- Size: Wingspans from about half an inch to almost 1 foot (30 cm)
- Life span: From about a week to several months as an adult

## Facts
- There are about 17,500 kinds of butterflies in the world.
- Butterflies live on every continent except Antarctica.
- A butterfly's life has four stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and adult butterfly.
- This amazing change is called metamorphosis.
- Caterpillars eat and eat and grow very quickly, shedding their skin several times.
- Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body turns into a butterfly.
- Butterflies have four wings: two front wings and two back wings.
- Butterfly wings are covered in thousands of tiny scales that give them their colors.
- Butterflies taste with their feet!
- Butterflies drink nectar from flowers through a long tube called a proboscis, like a straw.
- When a butterfly isn't drinking, it curls its proboscis up into a spiral.
- Butterflies help flowers grow by carrying pollen from one flower to another.
- Butterflies need warm sunshine to fly, so they often bask in the sun to warm up.
- Butterflies see colors that people can't see, including ultraviolet light.
- Monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles between Canada, the United States and Mexico.
- The monarch caterpillar eats only milkweed plants.
- Eating milkweed makes monarchs taste bad to birds, and their bright orange color is a warning.
- Some butterflies have spots on their wings that look like big eyes to scare away predators.
- The Queen Alexandra's birdwing is the largest butterfly, with wings almost 1 foot (30 cm) across.
- Some tiny butterflies have wings only about half an inch wide.
- The glasswing butterfly has see-through wings!
- Butterflies have two antennae with little knobs on the ends, which help them smell and balance.
- Many adult butterflies live only a few weeks, but some live for several months.
- Butterflies and moths are cousins. Most moths fly at night, while most butterflies fly in the daytime.
- Planting flowers like milkweed and lavender helps butterflies find food.

## Questions
Q: How does a caterpillar turn into a butterfly?
A: The caterpillar makes a chrysalis around itself. Inside, its body completely changes over a few weeks, and then a butterfly comes out. This is called metamorphosis.
Q: What do butterflies eat?
A: Adult butterflies drink sweet nectar from flowers using a straw-like tongue called a proboscis. Caterpillars eat leaves.
Q: How long do butterflies live?
A: Many butterflies live only a few weeks as adults, but some, like the monarchs that migrate, can live for several months.
Q: Why are butterflies colorful?
A: Their wings are covered in tiny scales. Bright colors can help butterflies find each other, warn predators that they taste bad, or help them hide.

---

# Horse Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/horse-facts-for-kids/

Horses are strong, fast and gentle animals that have been friends and helpers to people for thousands of years. They love to run, munch on grass and spend time with their herd. Let's gallop into some fun horse facts!

- Animal type: Mammal
- Home: Farms, ranches and grasslands all over the world
- Food: Grass, hay, oats and treats like apples and carrots
- Size: Measured in 'hands'; most horses are about 14 to 17 hands (4.7 to 5.7 feet) tall at the shoulder
- Life span: About 25 to 30 years

## Facts
- A baby horse is called a foal.
- A young female horse is called a filly, and a young male is called a colt.
- Foals can stand up and walk within about an hour of being born.
- Horses can sleep standing up, thanks to special locking joints in their legs.
- Horses also lie down for deep sleep, but usually only for a short time.
- Horses are measured in 'hands.' One hand is 4 inches (about 10 cm).
- A pony is a small horse that is under about 14.2 hands tall.
- There are hundreds of horse breeds, like Arabians, Clydesdales and Shetland ponies.
- Horses have the largest eyes of any land mammal.
- Because their eyes are on the sides of their heads, horses can see almost all the way around them.
- Horses can't breathe through their mouths, only through their noses.
- A horse's hooves are made of the same material as your fingernails, called keratin.
- Horseshoes protect a horse's hooves, a bit like shoes protect your feet.
- Horses can run at about 30 miles per hour (48 km/h) at a gallop.
- The four main ways horses move are walk, trot, canter and gallop.
- Horses are herbivores and love grass and hay.
- Horses can't burp or throw up!
- A horse's teeth keep growing, and grinding their food wears them down.
- You can guess a horse's age by looking at its teeth.
- Horses use their ears, eyes and nostrils to show how they feel.
- When a horse's ears are pointed forward, it is curious or interested.
- Horses live in groups called herds and like to have friends.
- Wild horses called mustangs roam the western United States.
- Horses have helped people farm, travel and deliver mail for thousands of years.
- Horses can remember people and places for many years.

## Questions
Q: What is a baby horse called?
A: A baby horse is called a foal. A young girl horse is a filly and a young boy horse is a colt.
Q: Do horses sleep standing up?
A: Yes, horses can doze standing up because their legs lock in place. They lie down for short periods of deep sleep.
Q: What do horses eat?
A: Horses mostly eat grass and hay. They also enjoy oats and treats like apples and carrots.
Q: What is the difference between a horse and a pony?
A: A pony is a small horse. Horses under about 14.2 hands (about 4 feet 10 inches) at the shoulder are usually called ponies.

---

# Rabbit Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/rabbit-facts-for-kids/

Rabbits are soft, fluffy animals with long ears, twitchy noses and powerful back legs for hopping. Whether they live in the wild or as pets, bunnies are full of surprises. Let's hop into some fun rabbit facts!

- Animal type: Mammal
- Home: Meadows, woods, deserts and grasslands on most continents; also pets at home
- Food: Grass, hay, leafy plants and vegetables
- Size: About 8 to 20 inches (20 to 50 cm) long for most kinds
- Life span: 1 to 2 years in the wild; 8 to 12 years as pets

## Facts
- A baby rabbit is called a kit or kitten.
- A girl rabbit is called a doe, and a boy rabbit is called a buck.
- Baby rabbits are born with their eyes closed and no fur.
- Rabbits can have several babies at once, called a litter.
- Wild rabbits often live in underground tunnels called warrens.
- A rabbit's teeth never stop growing, so they chew on hay and plants to keep them short.
- Rabbits are herbivores and eat grass, hay, leaves and vegetables.
- Carrots are a treat for rabbits, not their main food, because they are very sugary.
- Rabbits' long ears help them hear predators coming from far away.
- Rabbit ears also help them cool down when they get too warm.
- Rabbits can see almost all the way around them without turning their heads.
- A happy rabbit sometimes jumps and twists in the air. This is called a binky!
- Rabbits thump their back feet on the ground to warn others of danger.
- Some wild rabbits can run up to about 30 miles per hour (48 km/h) in short bursts.
- Rabbits zigzag when they run to escape from foxes and hawks.
- A rabbit's nose twitches to help it smell the air.
- Rabbits have whiskers that help them feel their way in the dark.
- Rabbits are most active at dawn and dusk.
- Rabbits and hares are cousins, but hares are bigger, have longer ears and are born with fur and open eyes.
- There are dozens of pet rabbit breeds, like Holland lops with floppy ears.
- The Flemish giant is one of the biggest rabbit breeds and can weigh over 7 kilograms (15 pounds).
- Rabbits can purr softly by rubbing their teeth together when they're content.
- Rabbits clean themselves often, a lot like cats do.
- Pet rabbits can learn their names and even use a litter box.
- Rabbits are social and are happiest with a rabbit friend.

## Questions
Q: What do rabbits eat?
A: Rabbits mostly eat grass and hay, plus leafy greens. Carrots and fruit are sweet treats to give only a little at a time.
Q: What is a baby rabbit called?
A: A baby rabbit is called a kit or kitten.
Q: Why do rabbits have big ears?
A: Big ears help rabbits hear predators from far away and also help them stay cool by releasing heat.
Q: What is the difference between a rabbit and a hare?
A: Hares are usually bigger with longer legs and ears. Baby hares are born with fur and open eyes, while baby rabbits are born without fur and with closed eyes.

---

# Hippo Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/hippo-facts-for-kids/

Hippos are huge, round animals that spend most of their day relaxing in rivers and lakes in Africa. Their name means 'river horse,' but they're more related to whales than horses! Let's splash into some fun hippo facts!

- Animal type: Mammal
- Home: Rivers, lakes and swamps in Africa
- Food: Mostly grass
- Size: About 11 to 16 feet (3.3 to 5 m) long
- Life span: About 40 to 50 years

## Facts
- The word hippopotamus means 'river horse' in ancient Greek.
- Hippos live in Africa, in rivers, lakes and swamps.
- Hippos are one of the largest land animals, after elephants and some rhinos.
- An adult hippo can weigh around 1,500 to 3,200 kilograms (3,300 to 7,000 pounds).
- Hippos spend up to 16 hours a day in the water to stay cool.
- Even though they live in water, hippos can't really swim. They walk or push off the bottom.
- A hippo can hold its breath underwater for about five minutes.
- Hippos can even sleep underwater and float up to breathe without waking up.
- Their eyes, ears and nostrils are on top of their heads, so they can see, hear and breathe while almost hidden in water.
- Hippos close their ears and nostrils when they go underwater.
- Hippos make a reddish oily liquid on their skin that works like sunscreen and helps keep their skin moist.
- At night, hippos come out of the water to eat grass.
- One hippo can eat around 35 to 40 kilograms (80 pounds) of grass in a night.
- Hippos can open their mouths very wide, nearly 180 degrees.
- A hippo's big tusk-like teeth keep growing all its life.
- Hippos look slow, but on land they can run about as fast as a person can sprint over short distances.
- A group of hippos is called a pod, a herd or a bloat.
- Baby hippos are called calves, and they are often born in the water.
- Baby hippos can drink milk underwater.
- Hippos 'talk' with grunts, honks and wheezes that can be heard far away.
- The closest living relatives of hippos are whales and dolphins.
- Pygmy hippos are a smaller kind that live in West African forests.
- Hippos are very protective of their space and can be dangerous to people, so they are best watched from far away.
- Birds sometimes ride on hippos' backs and eat bugs off their skin.
- Hippos help their river homes by fertilizing the water, which feeds fish and other animals.

## Questions
Q: Can hippos swim?
A: Not really! Hippos are too heavy to float well, so they walk along the bottom or bounce off it while holding their breath.
Q: What do hippos eat?
A: Hippos are herbivores. They come out at night to graze on grass and can eat around 80 pounds of it at a time.
Q: Where do hippos live?
A: Hippos live in Africa, in rivers, lakes and swamps where they can stay cool in the water during the day.
Q: Are hippos related to horses?
A: No. Even though their name means 'river horse,' hippos are most closely related to whales and dolphins.

---

# Gorilla Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/gorilla-facts-for-kids/

Gorillas are the largest apes in the world. They are strong but gentle, live in close family groups and are very smart. Let's swing into some amazing gorilla facts!

- Animal type: Mammal (great ape)
- Home: Forests of central Africa
- Food: Leaves, stems, fruit, bark and some insects
- Size: Adult males can stand about 5.5 feet (1.7 m) tall
- Life span: About 35 to 40 years in the wild

## Facts
- Gorillas are the biggest apes on Earth.
- There are two species of gorillas: eastern gorillas and western gorillas.
- Mountain gorillas are a kind of eastern gorilla that live in misty forests high in the mountains.
- Gorillas live in the forests of central Africa.
- Gorillas share about 98 percent of their DNA with people.
- Gorillas live in family groups called troops.
- A troop is led by a big adult male called a silverback.
- Silverbacks get their name from the silver-gray hair on their backs.
- Adult male gorillas can weigh about 140 to 200 kilograms (300 to 440 pounds).
- Gorillas mostly eat plants like leaves, stems, shoots and fruit.
- A big gorilla can eat around 18 kilograms (40 pounds) of plants in a day.
- Gorillas get most of the water they need from the plants they eat.
- Gorillas walk on all fours using their knuckles. This is called knuckle-walking.
- Every night, gorillas build a new nest out of leaves and branches to sleep in.
- Baby gorillas ride on their mothers' backs.
- A newborn gorilla weighs about 2 kilograms (4 to 5 pounds), a little less than many human babies.
- Young gorillas love to play, wrestle and chase each other.
- Gorillas beat their chests to communicate and show they are strong.
- Gorillas make many sounds, like grunts, hoots and even happy humming while they eat.
- Every gorilla has a unique nose print, like a human fingerprint.
- Gorillas are very smart and can use sticks as tools.
- Some gorillas living with people have learned to use sign language.
- Gorillas are gentle and shy and usually avoid trouble.
- All gorillas are endangered, mostly because their forest homes are being cut down.
- Protected parks and careful tourism help gorilla families grow.

## Questions
Q: How strong is a gorilla?
A: Gorillas are very strong. A silverback is many times stronger than an adult person, but gorillas are usually calm and gentle.
Q: What do gorillas eat?
A: Gorillas are mostly herbivores. They eat leaves, stems, shoots, fruit and bark, and sometimes ants and termites.
Q: What is a silverback?
A: A silverback is an adult male gorilla that leads the family troop. He gets his name from the silver hair on his back.
Q: Where do gorillas live?
A: Gorillas live in the rainforests and mountain forests of central Africa.

---

# Flamingo Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/flamingo-facts-for-kids/

Flamingos are bright pink birds with long legs and curvy necks. They stand on one leg, eat with their heads upside down and live in big noisy flocks. Let's wade into some fun flamingo facts!

- Animal type: Bird
- Home: Shallow lakes, lagoons and wetlands in Africa, Asia, Europe and the Americas
- Food: Tiny shrimp, algae and other small water creatures
- Size: About 3 to 5 feet (0.9 to 1.5 m) tall
- Life span: About 20 to 30 years in the wild

## Facts
- There are six kinds of flamingos.
- Flamingos live in Africa, Asia, Europe, South America and the Caribbean.
- Flamingos aren't born pink. Their chicks are gray or white.
- Flamingos turn pink from pigments in the algae and tiny shrimp they eat.
- The more of that food they eat, the brighter pink or orange they become.
- Flamingos often stand on one leg, which may help them save energy and stay warm.
- Flamingos eat with their heads upside down.
- Their beaks work like a strainer to filter tiny food out of the water and mud.
- What looks like a flamingo's knee bending backward is really its ankle. Its knee is hidden up near its body.
- Flamingos have webbed feet that help them walk on soft mud.
- Flamingos can fly, and they often travel at night.
- When flamingos fly, they stretch their necks forward and their legs out behind.
- Flamingos live in groups called flocks, and some flocks have thousands of birds.
- A group of flamingos is also called a flamboyance!
- Flamingos 'dance' together, marching and waving their heads in big groups.
- Flamingo parents build nests out of mud shaped like little volcanoes.
- A flamingo mom usually lays just one egg at a time.
- Both parents take turns keeping the egg warm.
- Flamingo parents feed their chick a special 'milk' made in their throats.
- Baby flamingos have straight beaks that start to curve as they grow.
- The greater flamingo is the biggest kind and can be about 5 feet (1.5 m) tall.
- The lesser flamingo is the smallest kind but the most common.
- Flamingos can live in salty or very alkaline lakes where few other animals can.
- Flamingos honk and grunt to talk with their flock.
- Some flamingos in zoos have lived for more than 50 years.

## Questions
Q: Why are flamingos pink?
A: Flamingos get their pink color from natural pigments in the algae and tiny shrimp they eat. Baby flamingos start out gray or white.
Q: Why do flamingos stand on one leg?
A: Scientists think standing on one leg helps flamingos save energy and stay warm by keeping one leg tucked under their body.
Q: What do flamingos eat?
A: Flamingos eat algae, tiny shrimp and other small creatures. They hold their heads upside down and use their beaks to strain food out of the water.
Q: Can flamingos fly?
A: Yes! Flamingos are strong fliers and often fly long distances at night.

---

# Bald Eagle Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/bald-eagle-facts-for-kids/

The bald eagle is a powerful bird of prey and the national bird of the United States. With its white head, sharp eyes and huge wings, it soars high over lakes and rivers looking for fish. Let's fly into some fun bald eagle facts!

- Animal type: Bird (bird of prey)
- Home: Near lakes, rivers and coasts across North America
- Food: Mostly fish, plus birds and small animals
- Size: Wingspan of about 6 to 7.5 feet (1.8 to 2.3 m)
- Life span: About 20 years or more in the wild

## Facts
- The bald eagle is the national bird of the United States.
- Bald eagles live only in North America.
- Bald eagles aren't really bald. 'Bald' comes from an old word meaning white-headed.
- Young bald eagles are mostly brown and don't get their white heads until they are about 5 years old.
- A bald eagle's wings can stretch about 6 to 7.5 feet (1.8 to 2.3 m) from tip to tip.
- Female bald eagles are bigger than males.
- Bald eagles have amazing eyesight and can spot a fish from very high in the sky.
- Their favorite food is fish, which they snatch from the water with their sharp talons.
- Bald eagles also eat birds, small mammals and sometimes steal food from other birds.
- A bald eagle's feet have rough bumps that help it hold slippery fish.
- Bald eagles build the biggest nests of any North American bird.
- Eagle pairs often use the same nest year after year and keep adding sticks to it.
- One famous bald eagle nest weighed about 2 tons, as much as a car!
- Bald eagle pairs usually stay together for life.
- Mother eagles usually lay one to three eggs.
- Both parents take turns keeping the eggs warm and feeding the chicks.
- Baby eagles are called eaglets.
- Eaglets are covered in fluffy gray down when they hatch.
- Young eagles learn to fly when they are about 10 to 12 weeks old.
- Bald eagles can soar for a long time on warm rising air without flapping their wings.
- Bald eagles have a surprisingly high, squeaky call.
- A bald eagle has around 7,000 feathers.
- Bald eagles were once in danger, but laws protecting them helped them make a huge comeback.
- Today, bald eagles are no longer endangered.
- Bald eagles can live 20 years or more in the wild.

## Questions
Q: Are bald eagles really bald?
A: No! Bald eagles have white feathers on their heads. The name comes from an old English word meaning white-headed.
Q: What do bald eagles eat?
A: Bald eagles mostly eat fish, which they grab from the water with their talons. They also eat birds and small animals.
Q: How big is a bald eagle?
A: Bald eagles are about 3 feet tall, and their wings can stretch 6 to 7.5 feet across.
Q: Why is the bald eagle the symbol of the United States?
A: The bald eagle was chosen as the national bird in 1782 because it is strong, free and found only in North America.

---

# Snake Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/snake-facts-for-kids/

Snakes are long, legless reptiles that slither, swim and even climb trees. Some are tiny and some are enormous, and most are completely harmless to people. Let's slither into some super snake facts!

- Animal type: Reptile
- Home: Every continent except Antarctica
- Food: Mice, birds, eggs, frogs, fish and insects
- Size: From about 4 inches (10 cm) to over 20 feet (6 m) long
- Life span: Often 10 to 30 years, depending on the kind

## Facts
- There are more than 3,900 kinds of snakes.
- Snakes live on every continent except Antarctica.
- Snakes are reptiles, which means they are cold-blooded and covered in scales.
- Snakes warm up by lying in the sun and cool down in the shade.
- Snakes don't have eyelids. A clear scale covers and protects each eye.
- Snakes smell with their tongues! They flick them out to collect smells from the air.
- Snakes don't have outside ears, but they can feel vibrations through the ground.
- Snakes shed their whole skin as they grow, often in one long piece.
- Snakes swallow their food whole because they can't chew.
- Stretchy jaws let snakes swallow animals bigger than their heads.
- After a big meal, some snakes don't need to eat again for weeks.
- Most snakes are not venomous, and many are harmless to people.
- Venomous snakes use special teeth called fangs.
- Pythons and boas squeeze their food instead of using venom.
- The reticulated python is the longest snake and can grow over 20 feet (6 m).
- The green anaconda is the heaviest snake in the world.
- The Barbados threadsnake is one of the smallest snakes and is only about 4 inches (10 cm) long.
- Some snakes lay eggs, and others give birth to live babies.
- Baby snakes are called snakelets or hatchlings.
- Rattlesnakes shake the rattle on their tails to warn others to stay away.
- Pit vipers can sense the body heat of animals, even in the dark.
- Some snakes can climb trees, and a few can even glide from branch to branch!
- Sea snakes spend almost their whole lives in the ocean.
- Snakes help farmers by eating mice and rats that damage crops.
- If you see a snake outside, the best thing to do is give it space and let a grown-up know.

## Questions
Q: How do snakes move without legs?
A: Snakes use strong muscles and belly scales that grip the ground. They push against bumps, curve side to side and stretch and bunch up to move along.
Q: Are all snakes dangerous?
A: No. Most snakes are not venomous and are harmless to people. Still, it's always best to leave wild snakes alone and tell a grown-up.
Q: Why do snakes flick their tongues?
A: Snakes smell with their tongues. They flick them to collect scents, then touch the tongue to a special smell organ in the roof of their mouth.
Q: What is the biggest snake?
A: The reticulated python is the longest snake, growing over 20 feet. The green anaconda is the heaviest.

---

# Spider Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/spider-facts-for-kids/

Spiders are eight-legged creatures that spin silk, build amazing webs and help keep bugs under control. They might look a little spooky, but most spiders are helpful friends. Let's creep into some cool spider facts!

- Animal type: Arachnid
- Home: Almost everywhere on land, on every continent except Antarctica
- Food: Insects and other small creatures
- Size: From smaller than a pinhead to about 11 inches (28 cm) across with legs
- Life span: About 1 to 2 years for most kinds; some tarantulas live 20 years or more

## Facts
- Spiders are not insects. They are arachnids.
- Insects have six legs, but spiders have eight.
- There are about 50,000 known kinds of spiders.
- Most spiders have eight eyes, but some have six, four, two or even none.
- All spiders can make silk.
- Pound for pound, spider silk can be stronger than steel.
- Spiders spin silk from body parts called spinnerets at the end of their bodies.
- Not all spiders build webs. Some hunt, jump or hide and wait.
- Orb-weaver spiders build round, wheel-shaped webs.
- Many orb-weavers build a brand new web every day.
- Spiders have tiny hairs on their legs that feel vibrations, so they know when something lands in their web.
- Spiders don't get stuck in their own webs because they walk on special non-sticky threads.
- Jumping spiders can leap many times the length of their own bodies.
- Jumping spiders have big front eyes and great eyesight.
- Baby spiders are called spiderlings.
- Some baby spiders travel by floating through the air on silk threads. This is called ballooning.
- Mother wolf spiders carry their babies on their backs.
- The Goliath birdeater is one of the biggest spiders, with legs about 11 inches (28 cm) across.
- Some spiders are smaller than the head of a pin.
- Spiders eat lots of insects, like flies and mosquitoes, which helps people.
- Tarantulas are big, hairy spiders that can live for many years.
- Most spiders are harmless to people, and only a few are dangerous.
- Spiders have been on Earth for hundreds of millions of years.
- A fear of spiders is called arachnophobia.
- Spiders are a favorite in nursery rhymes, like the Itsy Bitsy Spider who climbs up the water spout!

## Questions
Q: Is a spider an insect?
A: No. Spiders are arachnids. Insects have six legs and three body parts, while spiders have eight legs and two body parts.
Q: How do spiders make webs?
A: Spiders make silk inside their bodies and pull it out of spinnerets. They connect threads in patterns to make webs that catch insects.
Q: Why don't spiders stick to their own webs?
A: Spiders know which threads are sticky and walk on the dry ones. They also step carefully, using special hooked claws on their feet.
Q: Are spiders dangerous?
A: Most spiders are harmless and helpful because they eat pests. Only a few spiders can hurt people, so it's best not to touch wild spiders.

---

# Hedgehog Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/hedgehog-facts-for-kids/

Hedgehogs are small, spiky animals that roll into a prickly ball when they feel scared. They snuffle around at night looking for bugs to eat. Let's roll into some fun hedgehog facts!

- Animal type: Mammal
- Home: Gardens, hedges, woods and grasslands in Europe, Asia and Africa
- Food: Beetles, caterpillars, worms and other bugs
- Size: About 5 to 12 inches (13 to 30 cm) long
- Life span: About 2 to 5 years in the wild

## Facts
- There are 17 kinds of hedgehogs.
- Wild hedgehogs live in Europe, Asia and Africa, but not in the Americas.
- A hedgehog has about 5,000 to 7,000 spines on its back.
- Hedgehog spines are hollow hairs made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.
- Hedgehog spines aren't poisonous, and hedgehogs can't shoot them.
- When scared, a hedgehog rolls into a tight, spiky ball.
- Hedgehogs got their name because they like to live in hedges and make snorting, pig-like sounds.
- Hedgehogs are nocturnal, which means they are most active at night.
- Hedgehogs eat beetles, caterpillars, worms, slugs and other small creatures.
- Gardeners like hedgehogs because they eat bugs that damage plants.
- Hedgehogs have a great sense of smell and hearing, but not very good eyesight.
- A hedgehog can walk a mile or more in one night looking for food.
- Some hedgehogs hibernate in winter, sleeping in cozy nests of leaves.
- Baby hedgehogs are called hoglets.
- Hoglets are born with soft spines under their skin that pop out a few hours after birth.
- A group of hedgehogs is called an array.
- Hedgehogs sometimes lick strange smells and spread foamy spit on their spines. This is called self-anointing.
- Hedgehogs can swim and climb.
- Hedgehogs make snuffling, grunting and huffing sounds.
- The African pygmy hedgehog is a popular kind of pet hedgehog.
- Hedgehogs have been around for millions of years.
- Hedgehogs shouldn't drink milk because it gives them tummy aches.
- Leaving a small gap in a garden fence makes a 'hedgehog highway' so they can travel safely.
- Hedgehogs are mostly loners and like to live on their own.
- Some hedgehogs have spines that are white, brown or striped with both.

## Questions
Q: Why do hedgehogs have spikes?
A: Their spines protect them. When a hedgehog is scared, it curls into a ball so predators only see a prickly ball of spikes.
Q: What do hedgehogs eat?
A: Hedgehogs mostly eat insects and other small creatures, like beetles, caterpillars, worms and slugs.
Q: What is a baby hedgehog called?
A: A baby hedgehog is called a hoglet.
Q: Are hedgehogs nocturnal?
A: Yes. Hedgehogs sleep during the day and come out at night to search for food.

---

# Sea Otter Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/sea-otter-facts-for-kids/

Sea otters are playful ocean animals with the thickest fur in the world. They float on their backs, use rocks as tools and sometimes hold hands while they sleep! Let's float into some sweet sea otter facts!

- Animal type: Mammal
- Home: Coastal waters of the North Pacific Ocean
- Food: Sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels and fish
- Size: About 4 feet (1.2 m) long
- Life span: About 10 to 20 years

## Facts
- Sea otters live in the North Pacific Ocean, along the coasts of North America and Asia.
- Sea otters are one of the smallest marine mammals.
- Sea otters have the thickest fur of any animal, with up to about a million hairs per square inch.
- Unlike seals and whales, sea otters don't have a layer of blubber. Their fur keeps them warm.
- Sea otters spend lots of time grooming to keep their fur clean and fluffy.
- Sea otters spend most of their lives in the water.
- Sea otters float on their backs to eat, rest and groom.
- Sea otters use rocks as tools to crack open clams and shells.
- A sea otter has a pouch of loose skin under each arm to hold food and its favorite rock.
- Sea otters eat sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels and fish.
- Sea otters eat about a quarter of their body weight in food every day.
- Some sea otters hold hands or wrap themselves in kelp while they sleep so they don't drift away.
- A group of sea otters resting together in the water is called a raft.
- Baby sea otters are called pups.
- A mother sea otter carries her pup on her belly as she floats.
- Sea otter pups are so fluffy that they float like little corks.
- Sea otters can close their ears and nostrils when they dive.
- Sea otters can hold their breath for about five minutes.
- Sea otters have webbed back feet that work like flippers.
- Sea otters help kelp forests by eating sea urchins, which would otherwise munch the kelp.
- Healthy kelp forests are homes for many other ocean animals.
- Sea otters are a 'keystone species,' which means their ocean home depends on them.
- Long ago, sea otters were hunted for their fur until very few were left.
- Today, sea otters are protected, and their numbers have grown in many places.
- River otters are cousins of sea otters that live in rivers and lakes and spend more time on land.

## Questions
Q: Why do sea otters hold hands?
A: Sea otters sometimes hold hands or wrap themselves in kelp while sleeping so they don't float away from each other.
Q: How do sea otters stay warm?
A: Sea otters have the thickest fur of any animal. It traps air next to their skin and keeps the cold water out.
Q: What do sea otters eat?
A: Sea otters eat sea urchins, crabs, clams, mussels, snails and fish. They often use rocks to crack open hard shells.
Q: What is the difference between a sea otter and a river otter?
A: Sea otters live in the ocean and float on their backs, while river otters live in fresh water and spend more time on land.

---

# Red Fox Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/red-fox-facts-for-kids/

Red foxes are clever, quick animals with fluffy tails and pointy ears. They live in forests, fields and even cities, and they can hear a mouse squeak from far away. Let's trot into some fun red fox facts!

- Animal type: Mammal
- Home: Forests, grasslands, mountains, deserts and cities across North America, Europe, Asia and North Africa
- Food: Mice, rabbits, birds, insects, fruit and berries
- Size: About 3 to 4 feet (0.9 to 1.2 m) long, including the tail
- Life span: About 2 to 5 years in the wild

## Facts
- Red foxes live in more places around the world than almost any other wild meat-eating mammal.
- Foxes are part of the dog family, along with wolves and coyotes.
- Red foxes aren't always red. Some are black, silver or a mix called 'cross' foxes.
- Most red foxes have a white tip on their bushy tails.
- A fox's tail is called a brush.
- Foxes wrap their fluffy tails around themselves like a blanket to stay warm.
- A male fox is called a dog or a tod, and a female is called a vixen.
- Baby foxes are called kits, cubs or pups.
- Fox families live in dens, which are often underground burrows.
- Red foxes have amazing hearing and can hear small animals moving under the snow.
- In winter, foxes leap high into the air and pounce headfirst into the snow to catch mice.
- Scientists think foxes may use Earth's magnetic field to aim their pounces.
- Foxes are omnivores, so they eat both animals and plants.
- Red foxes eat mice, rabbits, birds, insects, fruit and berries.
- Foxes sometimes bury extra food to eat later. This is called caching.
- Foxes have whiskers on their faces and legs to help them feel their way.
- Red foxes can run about 30 miles per hour (48 km/h).
- Foxes make lots of sounds, including barks, yips and even screams.
- Foxes have vertical, slit-shaped pupils, a bit like a cat's.
- Red foxes are mostly active at dusk, at night and at dawn.
- Many red foxes have learned to live in big cities, like London.
- Foxes usually hunt alone instead of in packs.
- Fox parents both help raise their kits.
- Fox kits start exploring outside the den when they are about a month old.
- The arctic fox is a cousin of the red fox that turns white in winter.

## Questions
Q: What do red foxes eat?
A: Red foxes are omnivores. They eat mice, voles, rabbits, birds and insects, plus fruit and berries.
Q: Are foxes dogs or cats?
A: Foxes belong to the dog family, but they have some cat-like habits, like pouncing on prey and having slit-shaped pupils.
Q: What is a baby fox called?
A: A baby fox is called a kit, cub or pup.
Q: Why do foxes jump into the snow?
A: Foxes hear mice moving under the snow, then leap high and dive headfirst to catch them. This is called mousing.

---

# Squirrel Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/squirrel-facts-for-kids/

Squirrels are busy, bushy-tailed animals that scamper up trees, leap between branches and bury nuts for later. You can probably spot one in a park near you! Let's scurry into some super squirrel facts!

- Animal type: Mammal (rodent)
- Home: Forests, parks and cities on every continent except Australia and Antarctica
- Food: Nuts, seeds, acorns, fruit, mushrooms and buds
- Size: From about 3 inches to over 3 feet (1 m) long, depending on the kind
- Life span: About 5 to 10 years

## Facts
- There are more than 250 kinds of squirrels.
- Squirrels live on every continent except Australia and Antarctica.
- There are three main groups: tree squirrels, ground squirrels and flying squirrels.
- Chipmunks, marmots and prairie dogs are all part of the squirrel family.
- Squirrels are rodents, like mice and beavers.
- A squirrel's front teeth never stop growing, so chewing nuts keeps them short.
- Squirrels bury nuts and seeds to eat during winter.
- A squirrel can bury thousands of nuts in a single season.
- Squirrels use their great sense of smell, and their memory, to find buried food.
- Forgotten nuts can grow into new trees, so squirrels help plant forests!
- Some squirrels pretend to bury a nut to trick anyone who is watching.
- Squirrels can turn their back feet around to climb down trees headfirst.
- A squirrel's bushy tail helps it balance, keeps it warm and acts like an umbrella.
- Squirrels flick their tails to send messages to other squirrels.
- Flying squirrels don't really fly. They glide from tree to tree using flaps of skin.
- Some flying squirrels can glide around 150 feet (45 m) in one leap.
- Baby squirrels are called kits or kittens.
- Squirrel nests in trees are called dreys, and they are made of twigs and leaves.
- Squirrels can jump about 10 times the length of their bodies.
- Squirrels have sharp claws that grip tree bark.
- The African pygmy squirrel is tiny, only about 3 inches (7.5 cm) long without its tail.
- The Indian giant squirrel can be over 3 feet (1 m) long, including its tail, and has colorful fur.
- Ground squirrels live in underground tunnels.
- Squirrels chatter, squeak and bark to warn each other about danger.
- Squirrels are very good at solving puzzles to reach bird feeders!

## Questions
Q: What do squirrels eat?
A: Squirrels mostly eat nuts, seeds, acorns, fruit, mushrooms and tree buds. Some also eat insects and eggs.
Q: Why do squirrels bury nuts?
A: Squirrels bury food to save it for winter when food is hard to find. The nuts they forget can grow into new trees.
Q: Can flying squirrels really fly?
A: No, flying squirrels glide. They stretch out flaps of skin between their legs and sail from tree to tree.
Q: What is a squirrel's nest called?
A: A squirrel's nest in a tree is called a drey. It's made of twigs, leaves and moss.

---

# Duck Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/duck-facts-for-kids/

Ducks are water birds that quack, waddle and paddle around ponds and lakes. They have waterproof feathers and webbed feet that make them great swimmers. Let's paddle into some fun duck facts!

- Animal type: Bird
- Home: Ponds, lakes, rivers, marshes and coasts on every continent except Antarctica
- Food: Water plants, seeds, insects, snails and small fish
- Size: From about 12 inches to over 2 feet (30 to 70 cm) long
- Life span: About 5 to 10 years in the wild

## Facts
- There are more than 100 kinds of ducks.
- Ducks live on every continent except Antarctica.
- A male duck is called a drake, and a female duck is called a hen.
- Baby ducks are called ducklings.
- Ducklings can swim soon after they hatch.
- Ducklings follow the first moving thing they see, usually their mother. This is called imprinting.
- Ducks have webbed feet that work like paddles.
- Ducks have special oil glands near their tails to make their feathers waterproof.
- Water rolls right off a duck's back, which is where the saying comes from!
- Ducks' feet don't feel very cold because of special blood vessels that keep heat in.
- Not all ducks quack. Many ducks whistle, coo, grunt or squeak.
- Usually it's female mallards that make the loud 'quack' sound.
- Dabbling ducks, like mallards, tip their bottoms up to eat plants under the water.
- Diving ducks swim all the way underwater to find food.
- Ducks eat water plants, seeds, insects, snails, worms and small fish.
- Bread isn't good for ducks. Peas, corn and oats are healthier treats.
- Male mallards have shiny green heads, while females are speckled brown.
- The wood duck is one of the most colorful ducks in North America.
- Wood duck ducklings jump out of tree nests, sometimes from high up, to reach the water!
- Many ducks fly south in a V shape when the weather gets cold.
- Ducks can sleep with one eye open to watch for danger.
- Ducks have three eyelids.
- Mother ducks line their nests with soft feathers from their own chests.
- A group of ducks on the water is sometimes called a raft or a paddling.
- Nursery rhymes love ducks, like the Five Little Ducks who went swimming one day!

## Questions
Q: What is a baby duck called?
A: A baby duck is called a duckling. A male duck is a drake and a female duck is a hen.
Q: Do all ducks quack?
A: No! Many ducks whistle, coo or grunt. The classic loud quack usually comes from female mallards.
Q: What do ducks eat?
A: Ducks eat water plants, seeds, grass, insects, snails, worms and small fish. Bread isn't healthy for them.
Q: Why don't ducks get wet?
A: Ducks spread oil from a gland near their tail over their feathers, which makes them waterproof.

---

# Sheep Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/sheep-facts-for-kids/

Sheep are fluffy farm animals famous for their soft, warm wool. They say 'baa,' stick together in flocks and have lived alongside people for thousands of years. Let's baa into some fun sheep facts!

- Animal type: Mammal
- Home: Farms and grassy hills all over the world
- Food: Grass, clover, hay and other plants
- Size: About 4 to 6 feet (1.2 to 1.8 m) long
- Life span: About 10 to 12 years

## Facts
- A female sheep is called a ewe, a male sheep is called a ram, and a baby is called a lamb.
- The word sheep is the same whether you mean one sheep or many sheep.
- A group of sheep is called a flock.
- There are more than 1,000 breeds of sheep.
- People have raised sheep for about 10,000 years.
- Sheep's wool keeps growing, so most farm sheep need a haircut called shearing once a year.
- One sheep's wool can be made into several sweaters!
- Wool is made of keratin, like your hair and nails.
- Wool is naturally waterproof because of an oily substance called lanolin.
- Lanolin is used to make some soaps and lotions.
- Sheep are herbivores and eat grass, clover, hay and other plants.
- Sheep have four parts to their stomachs, which helps them digest grass.
- Sheep chew their food twice! They bring it back up and chew it again. This is called chewing the cud.
- Sheep have rectangle-shaped pupils that help them see almost all the way around without turning their heads.
- Sheep can recognize the faces of many other sheep and even people.
- Sheep feel safer in a flock and follow each other closely.
- Lambs can stand and walk within minutes of being born.
- A mother sheep knows her lamb by its voice and smell.
- Rams of some breeds have big, curly horns.
- Bighorn sheep live wild in the mountains of North America and are great climbers.
- Sheepdogs help farmers move flocks of sheep from place to place.
- Sheep don't have top front teeth, just a hard pad on top.
- Some sheep are raised for milk, which can be made into cheese like feta.
- Sheep can be black, brown, white or spotted.
- Sheep are stars of nursery rhymes, like Baa Baa Black Sheep and Mary Had a Little Lamb!

## Questions
Q: What is a baby sheep called?
A: A baby sheep is called a lamb. A mother sheep is a ewe and a father sheep is a ram.
Q: Why do sheep need to be sheared?
A: Most farm sheep grow wool all year and can't shed it on their own, so farmers give them a haircut called shearing to keep them cool and comfortable.
Q: What do sheep eat?
A: Sheep are herbivores. They graze on grass and clover and eat hay in winter.
Q: Are sheep smart?
A: Yes! Sheep can recognize dozens of faces, remember them for years and learn their way around.

---

# Camel Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/camel-facts-for-kids/

Camels are tough desert animals with humps on their backs and long eyelashes to keep sand out. They can go a long time without water and carry heavy loads across the hot desert. Let's trek into some fun camel facts!

- Animal type: Mammal
- Home: Deserts and dry lands of Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Australia
- Food: Desert plants, grass, leaves and even thorny shrubs
- Size: About 6 to 7 feet (1.8 to 2.1 m) tall at the hump
- Life span: About 40 years

## Facts
- There are two main kinds of camels: dromedaries with one hump and Bactrian camels with two humps.
- A fun way to remember: a dromedary's hump makes a 'D' shape, and a Bactrian's two humps make a 'B' shape lying on its side.
- Camel humps store fat, not water.
- The fat in the hump gives camels energy when food is hard to find.
- Camels can go a week or more without drinking water.
- A very thirsty camel can drink about 100 liters (over 25 gallons) of water in a short time.
- Camels have two rows of long eyelashes to keep sand out of their eyes.
- Camels can close their nostrils to keep out blowing sand.
- Camels have wide, padded feet that help them walk on soft sand without sinking.
- Camels have thick pads on their knees so they can kneel on hot ground.
- Camels' body temperature can change during the day to help them save water.
- Camels eat thorny desert plants that most animals can't, thanks to their tough mouths.
- A baby camel is called a calf.
- Baby camels are born without humps.
- Camels can carry heavy loads for long distances across the desert.
- Camels have been called 'ships of the desert.'
- Camels can run about 40 miles per hour (65 km/h) in short sprints.
- Camels walk by moving both legs on one side of their body at the same time, which makes them sway.
- Bactrian camels live in cold deserts and grow thick shaggy coats in winter.
- Wild Bactrian camels are very rare and live in the Gobi Desert of China and Mongolia.
- Camels grunt, moan and bellow to communicate.
- Camel milk is a healthy drink for many people in desert countries.
- There are many wild camels in Australia, brought there over 150 years ago.
- Llamas and alpacas are cousins of camels from South America.
- Alice the Camel from the song has five humps, but real camels only have one or two!

## Questions
Q: Do camels store water in their humps?
A: No. Camel humps store fat, which the camel can use for energy. Camels can still go a long time without water because their bodies save it very well.
Q: How many humps do camels have?
A: Dromedary camels have one hump and Bactrian camels have two humps.
Q: How long can a camel go without water?
A: Camels can go a week or more without drinking, and even longer if they eat juicy plants.
Q: What is a baby camel called?
A: A baby camel is called a calf. Calves are born without humps.

---

# Chicken Facts for Kids
URL: https://plooshi.com/chicken-facts-for-kids/

Chickens are friendly farm birds that cluck, scratch and lay eggs. There are more chickens in the world than any other bird! Let's peck into some egg-cellent chicken facts!

- Animal type: Bird
- Home: Farms and backyards all over the world
- Food: Seeds, grains, bugs, worms and plants
- Size: Most are about 16 to 28 inches (40 to 70 cm) tall
- Life span: About 5 to 10 years

## Facts
- There are more chickens in the world than any other kind of bird.
- A female chicken is called a hen, and a male chicken is called a rooster.
- Baby chickens are called chicks.
- Chickens came from a wild bird called the red junglefowl in Asia.
- Chickens are distant relatives of dinosaurs, like the T. rex!
- Hens can lay eggs without a rooster, but those eggs won't hatch into chicks.
- Many hens lay about one egg a day.
- Egg shells can be white, brown, blue or green, depending on the breed.
- A chick takes about 21 days to hatch from its egg.
- Chicks use a tiny bump on their beaks called an egg tooth to break out of the shell.
- A mother hen clucks to her eggs, and the chicks can peep back from inside the shell.
- Roosters crow in the morning, but they also crow at other times of the day.
- Chickens can make dozens of different sounds to talk with each other.
- Chickens have a 'pecking order,' which is a ranking of who is in charge of the flock.
- Chickens can fly a little, but only short distances.
- Chickens love dust baths! Rolling in dirt helps keep their feathers clean and bugs away.
- Chickens are omnivores and eat seeds, grains, insects, worms and plants.
- Chickens don't have teeth. They swallow small stones that help grind food in their gizzard.
- Chickens can see more colors than people can.
- Chickens can recognize many other chickens and people.
- The red part on top of a chicken's head is called a comb.
- The red flaps under a chicken's beak are called wattles.
- Silkie chickens have fluffy feathers that feel like fur.
- Some chickens like to be petted and can be very friendly pets.
- Chickens sleep on perches called roosts and tuck their heads under their wings.

## Questions
Q: What is a baby chicken called?
A: A baby chicken is called a chick. A mother chicken is a hen and a father chicken is a rooster.
Q: How long does it take a chicken egg to hatch?
A: A chicken egg takes about 21 days to hatch when it is kept warm by a hen or an incubator.
Q: Can chickens fly?
A: Chickens can fly a little, usually just short hops up onto fences or perches.
Q: Are chickens related to dinosaurs?
A: Yes! Birds, including chickens, evolved from small feathered dinosaurs.
